body:
Meaning of resource efficiency

Resource efficiency means obtaining more useful goods, services or benefits from available resources, or providing the same benefit with fewer resource inputs and less waste. It applies to households, farms, industries, cities and entire economies.

Efficiency should not be confused with simply reducing expenditure. A cheap process may use excessive water, energy or materials, while a more resource-efficient process may require greater initial investment but consume fewer resources during operation.

Resource productivity

Resource productivity compares useful output with the quantity of resource used. A higher ratio generally means that more output is obtained from each unit of input.

Resource productivity = Useful output divided by Resource input.

Output can be measured in physical units, such as kilograms of crops, or economic units, such as value added. The meaning of the ratio depends on the chosen output and input measures.

The 4 major resource dimensions

ResourceMeaning of productivityPractical improvement
MaterialsUseful output or economic value per unit of material inputReduce manufacturing scrap and reuse suitable components
WaterUseful output per unit of water used or consumed, as defined by the indicatorRepair leaks and reuse suitably treated water
EnergyUseful output or service per unit of energy consumedUse efficient motors and avoid unnecessary operation
LandUseful output per unit of land areaImprove existing land use without unnecessary expansion

Material productivity

An industrial unit improves material productivity when it manufactures the same quantity and quality of goods using less raw material. Better cutting patterns, reduced rejection rates and reuse of production scrap can contribute.

At the national level, a commonly used economic indicator is GDP divided by Domestic Material Consumption (DMC). It expresses economic output per unit of material directly used in the economy. This economic ratio is useful, but GDP alone does not measure environmental quality or social well-being.

Water productivity

A farmer may improve water productivity by obtaining a similar crop yield while reducing water consumed through evaporation and plant transpiration. Industries may reduce freshwater withdrawals through leak prevention, process changes and reuse of suitably treated wastewater.

Water withdrawal is water taken from a source. Water consumption is the portion not returned to the same water system in a usable form during the relevant accounting period, such as water evaporated or incorporated into products. Therefore, water withdrawal and water consumption should not be treated as identical.

Energy productivity

Energy productivity rises when more goods or services are produced per unit of energy input. Efficient motors, improved insulation and better process control can reduce energy requirements.

Energy efficiency and renewable energy serve different purposes. An efficient coal-powered process may still depend on fossil fuel. A solar-powered process may use renewable electricity but still waste energy if equipment is poorly operated.

Land productivity

Land productivity can be expressed as crop output per hectare or another suitable measure of useful output per unit of land. Higher agricultural productivity may reduce pressure to cultivate additional land, but only when associated effects are also considered. Heavy groundwater extraction, soil degradation or excessive chemical use may undermine long-term sustainability despite high short-term yields.

Renewable resource use must remain sustainable

Renewability does not guarantee unlimited availability. A forest can regenerate, but not necessarily as fast as trees are removed. An aquifer can recharge, but withdrawals may exceed recharge. Sustainable management therefore considers the rate of resource renewal and the environmental impacts of use.

Relative and absolute decoupling

Decoupling means reducing the connection between economic growth and environmental resource pressure.

  • Relative decoupling: Resource use grows more slowly than economic output.
  • Absolute decoupling: Resource use remains constant or falls while economic output rises.

Consider a hypothetical economy with an output index of 100 and a material-use index of 100. Later, output rises to 120. If material use rises to 110, material use is increasing more slowly than output: this is relative decoupling. If material use instead falls to 90 while output rises to 120, this is absolute decoupling.

These figures are illustrative, not measured data. A higher resource-productivity ratio does not by itself establish absolute decoupling.

Efficiency is not the same as sustainability. A factory may become more material-efficient while expanding production so rapidly that its total material consumption still rises. Both resource use per unit of output and total resource use matter.

Prelims focus

  • Resource productivity compares useful output with resource input.
  • A common economy-wide material-productivity indicator is GDP divided by DMC.
  • Water withdrawal and water consumption are not identical.
  • Relative decoupling permits resource use to rise more slowly than economic output.
  • Absolute decoupling requires resource use to remain constant or fall while economic output rises.
  • Trap: Higher efficiency does not necessarily mean lower total resource consumption.

[Sources: NCERT, Resources and Development, Class 8 Geography, Chapter 1, 'Resources', printed pp. 3–6; NCERT, Indian Economic Development, Class 11 Economics, Chapter 9, 'Environment and Sustainable Development', sections 9.2 and 9.4; United Nations Statistics Division, 'SDG Report 2025', Goal 12, section on domestic material consumption; European Environment Agency, materials on resource productivity and relative and absolute decoupling, consulted 1 November 2026; Water Footprint Network, The Water Footprint Assessment Manual, section on water consumption.]

pictures.alt: Output rises from 100 to 120 in both cases; material use rises to 110 in relative decoupling and falls to 90 in absolute decoupling.
pictures.caption: Economic output can rise while material use rises more slowly or falls.

title: Resource Efficiency: Material, Water, Energy and Land Productivity

body:
Connecting the resource flows of different industries

Factories commonly obtain raw materials, water and energy and then produce goods, by-products and waste. One factory may discard a substance that another factory could use as an input.

Industrial symbiosis

Industrial symbiosis is cooperation among enterprises through which suitable materials, by-products, water or energy streams from one operation are used beneficially by another. The purpose is to reduce waste, demand for virgin inputs and environmental burdens.

The term refers to a useful exchange or cooperation, not merely the presence of several factories in the same industrial estate. Industries may be located close together, but location alone does not establish industrial symbiosis.

Typical industrial exchanges

  • By-product use: Suitable fly ash from a coal-based thermal power plant can be used as a material in certain cement and construction products, subject to technical and environmental requirements.
  • Water reuse: Treated wastewater from one system can replace freshwater for an industrial application when its quality meets the required standard.
  • Waste-heat use: Usable heat from a production process can supply another process or heating requirement.
  • Organic residue use: Suitable agricultural or food-processing residues can become inputs for composting or biogas production.

These exchanges reduce waste only when they are properly managed. A material containing dangerous contaminants must not be redirected into another product merely to avoid disposal. Quality control, reliable supply, transport requirements and compliance with applicable standards are essential.

Resource-efficient and cleaner production

Cleaner production seeks to prevent pollution and waste within a production process. It may involve modifying equipment, reducing material losses, substituting safer inputs or recovering resources internally.

This differs from an exclusively end-of-pipe approach, in which pollutants are treated after they have already been generated. Wastewater treatment remains important, but preventing unnecessary water use or contamination can reduce the burden placed on treatment systems.

Circular business models

A business model affects how products are sold, used, maintained and returned. Several models support circularity:

ModelHow it worksCircular benefit
Repair and resaleUsed products are serviced and sold for further use.Extends product life
Sharing or rentalSeveral users access the same equipment at different times.May reduce the need for separate products
Product-as-a-serviceA customer pays for a service rather than buying the equipment outright.Can encourage maintenance and efficient use
Take-back systemUsed products or packaging return through an organised collection channel.Supports reuse and recovery

For example, a provider that retains ownership of industrial equipment may have an incentive to design it for long life and maintain it regularly. However, such environmental benefits are possible outcomes, not automatic guarantees. The business model must actually reduce resource use and waste.

Gujarat example: treated wastewater as a resource in Surat

Surat provides a concrete example of urban-industrial resource circularity. Instead of treating municipal wastewater only as a disposal problem, the city has developed treatment infrastructure to make water suitable for specified non-potable uses.

According to a Press Information Bureau release dated 24 September 2024, Surat Municipal Corporation had established 4 tertiary treatment plants with a combined installed capacity of 116 million litres per day (MLD). The release described reuse of treated wastewater for industrial purposes, lake rejuvenation, agriculture, plantations, sewer cleaning and gardening.

The figure of 116 MLD describes installed treatment capacity reported on 24 September 2024. It should not be interpreted as a verified daily quantity reused, or as an independently verified operating capacity on 1 November 2026.

This example illustrates how treated wastewater can substitute for freshwater in appropriate applications. The treatment level and intended use must match; water suitable for an industrial process is not automatically suitable for drinking.

Relationship with eco-industrial parks

An eco-industrial park promotes improved environmental performance through cleaner production, efficient management of energy and water, pollution prevention and cooperation among enterprises. Industrial symbiosis is an important possible component of such a park, but an eco-industrial park also requires broader environmental management.

Prelims focus

  • Industrial symbiosis involves useful exchanges of materials, water, energy or by-products among enterprises.
  • Co-location of factories alone does not establish industrial symbiosis.
  • Cleaner production emphasizes preventing pollution and resource losses.
  • Product-as-a-service can create incentives for maintenance and durability.
  • A PIB release dated 24 September 2024 reported 4 tertiary treatment plants in Surat with a combined installed capacity of 116 MLD.
  • Trap: Installed treatment capacity is not the same as the volume of water actually reused.

[Sources: United Nations Industrial Development Organization, An International Framework for Eco-Industrial Parks, Version 2.0, section 4.4, 'Environmental Performance Requirements', 2021; NCERT, Biology, Class 12, Chapter 16, 'Environmental Issues', section 16.4, case study of integrated organic farming; Press Information Bureau, Ahmedabad, 'Surat Municipal Corporation has converted the wastewater generated in the city into the resource by establishing 4 Tertiary Treatment Plants', 24 September 2024, Release ID 2058237; sources consulted 1 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Four exchanges turn fly ash, treated wastewater, waste heat and organic residues into useful inputs, subject to suitability, treatment and environmental safeguards.
pictures.caption: Industrial symbiosis creates useful connections among material, water and energy flows.

pictures.alt: A wastewater-treatment facility in Surat with tanks, water channels and teal pipelines carrying treated water to nearby factories for reuse.
pictures.caption: Treated municipal wastewater can supply suitable non-potable uses and reduce freshwater demand.

title: Industrial Symbiosis, Circular Business Models and the Gujarat Experience

body:
Why the use stage is only part of the environmental impact

A product can appear environmentally friendly during use while causing significant impacts during extraction or manufacturing. Similarly, a product made from recycled material may still require substantial energy for processing and transport.

Life-cycle thinking examines environmental effects across the successive stages of a product's existence rather than judging it by only one stage.

Stages in a product's life cycle

  1. Resource extraction: Natural materials are obtained, such as minerals, timber or agricultural raw materials.
  2. Processing and manufacture: Raw materials are processed and assembled into products.
  3. Distribution: Products are packaged, stored and transported.
  4. Use and maintenance: Consumers or businesses operate, clean, maintain and repair the products.
  5. End-of-life management: Products may be reused, refurbished, remanufactured, recycled, recovered or disposed of.

These stages interact. A design choice that reduces material use during manufacture might shorten product life, while a longer-lasting product may require more material initially but need fewer replacements.

Life-cycle thinking and Life Cycle Assessment

Life Cycle Assessment (LCA) is a systematic method for assessing potential environmental impacts associated with a product system across defined life-cycle stages. It considers relevant inputs, outputs and environmental effects.

Life-cycle thinking is the broader way of considering these connections. A formal LCA uses a stated scope and assessment method to analyse them.

Two useful terms are:

  • Cradle-to-gate: Assessment from raw material extraction through production until the product leaves a defined production facility.
  • Cradle-to-grave: Assessment from raw material extraction through use and final end-of-life treatment or disposal.

An LCA comparison also needs a common functional unit, meaning the service being compared. For example, comparing 1 disposable drinking cup with 1 reusable cup without considering repeated use may be misleading. A more meaningful comparison would examine the environmental impact of providing a specified number of drinks under the relevant conditions.

Environmental trade-offs and burden shifting

An environmental improvement in one stage may increase impacts in another. Replacing a material with a lighter alternative may reduce transport fuel consumption but make the product more difficult to recycle. Reusable packaging may avoid repeated manufacture of disposable packaging but require water and energy for cleaning.

Such effects are called trade-offs or, when an impact is moved rather than genuinely reduced, burden shifting. Life-cycle thinking helps identify these effects.

A claim that a product is better because it uses less plastic, contains recycled material or is reusable does not by itself establish that its total environmental impact is lower. The result depends on the materials, production processes, number of uses, energy sources and end-of-life conditions.

What is the rebound effect?

Efficiency improvements reduce the resource required for a particular service. They may also reduce the cost of that service. When lower costs encourage additional consumption, some of the expected resource savings can be lost. This is the rebound effect.

Direct rebound effect

Suppose an air conditioner becomes more energy-efficient. Its owner may then operate it for longer periods because cooling costs less per hour. The extra use directly offsets some of the potential electricity saving.

Indirect rebound effect

A household may save money by purchasing an energy-efficient appliance and spend part of those savings on other goods or activities that require resources. The additional environmental impact occurs indirectly.

A numerical example

Consider a hypothetical device that initially consumes 1 kWh for each unit of service. It provides 100 units of service, so its total consumption is 100 kWh.

After an efficiency improvement, consumption falls to 0.6 kWh per unit of service. If usage remains at 100 units, consumption would be 60 kWh, a 40% reduction.

However, if usage rises to 150 units, actual consumption becomes 90 kWh. The efficiency improvement remains real, but the total saving is only 10% compared with the original 100 kWh.

A rebound effect does not mean that every efficiency improvement increases total consumption. The magnitude depends on prices, behaviour, income and other conditions. In an extreme case, increased total resource use despite improved efficiency is associated with the Jevons paradox.

Prelims focus

  • Life-cycle thinking covers extraction, manufacture, distribution, use and end-of-life management.
  • LCA is a systematic assessment of potential environmental impacts across a defined product system.
  • Cradle-to-gate generally stops at the factory gate; cradle-to-grave includes use and final treatment.
  • A functional unit defines the service used for comparison.
  • Direct rebound involves greater use of the more efficient service; indirect rebound involves additional consumption elsewhere.
  • Trap: The rebound effect does not necessarily eliminate all efficiency gains.

[Sources: United Nations Environment Programme, A Policymakers' Guide to Life Cycle Assessment, policy brief, November 2024, overview of life-cycle stages, impacts and trade-offs; European Environment Agency, 'Accelerating the energy efficiency renovation of residential buildings — a behavioural approach', section 'What happens after renovation? Behavioural insights and the rebound effect', consulted 1 November 2026; NCERT, Indian Economic Development, Class 11 Economics, Chapter 9, sections 9.2 and 9.4.]

pictures.caption: Life-cycle thinking includes impacts before use, during use and after use.

title: Life-Cycle Thinking, Environmental Trade-offs and Rebound Effects
